research_question: Does resistance training delivered during anticancer therapy, compared with no training (usual care/waitlist/non-exercise control), reduce cancer-related fatigue assessed at 12 weeks or less in people with cancer?
control_label: No training (usual care, waitlist, or non-exercise control)
outcome_description: Cancer-related fatigue measured with any validated self-report instrument (e.g. FACIT-F/FACT-F fatigue subscale, EORTC QLQ-C30 fatigue scale, Brief Fatigue Inventory, Piper Fatigue Scale, MFI, FSI, POMS fatigue subscale) at a post-intervention or follow-up assessment occurring 12 weeks or less from baseline/randomization. Scores are oriented so that higher = more fatigue (reverse-oriented scales such as FACIT-F are rescored accordingly).
positive_direction: A positive Hedges g / SMD means the resistance training group had LESS cancer-related fatigue than the no-training control group (i.e. resistance training reduced fatigue).
search_queries: resistance training cancer-related fatigue randomized controlled trial
strength training during chemotherapy fatigue outcome patients with cancer
progressive resistance exercise radiotherapy fatigue trial effect
inclusion_criteria: Participants are people diagnosed with any type or stage of cancer who are undergoing anticancer therapy (chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormonal, targeted, or immunotherapy) during the intervention period

The study evaluates a resistance/strength training intervention (alone or as a clearly identifiable component of an exercise programme) compared with a non-exercising control group such as usual care, waitlist, attention control, or stretching/education only

The study reports some quantitative measure of fatigue at an assessment point of 12 weeks or less from baseline (means and SDs, change scores, t/F statistics, or other data from which an effect size can be derived)
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic review, meta-analysis, editorial, commentary, opinion piece, protocol, conference abstract without data, or purely theoretical/narrative paper)
No comparison between a resistance-training condition and a non-training control condition (e.g. single-arm pre-post studies, or comparisons only between two active exercise arms)
No quantitative fatigue outcome data from which an effect size can be computed (no means+SDs, t/F values, proportions, or odds ratios reported or derivable)

Fatigue reported only at follow-up windows later than 12 weeks post-baseline, or the study is completely unrelated to resistance training and cancer-related fatigue (e.g. non-cancer populations, no fatigue outcome)
moderators_to_extract: Cancer type (breast, prostate, mixed, haematological, other)
Type of anticancer therapy during the intervention (chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormonal/other)
Intervention modality (resistance training only vs combined aerobic + resistance)
Supervision and setting (supervised in-person, home-based/unsupervised, hybrid)
Intervention duration and weekly session frequency/dose
Fatigue instrument used (FACIT-F, EORTC QLQ-C30, BFI, PFS, MFI, other)
Sample size category and risk-of-bias/attrition level
effect_size_note: Pool as standardized mean difference (Hedges g-corrected SMD) because studies use heterogeneous fatigue instruments. Where only change-from-baseline means are available, compute SMD from change scores using baseline or pooled SDs. Reverse the sign for scales where higher = better (e.g. FACIT-F, FACT-F, EORTC functional orientation) so that a positive effect always indicates less fatigue with resistance training. Random-effects (REML) model with Knapp-Hartung adjustment; heterogeneity via tau-squared and I-squared; publication bias via funnel plot and Egger's test.
